sections.title: Poster Title Info
sections.content: Robust Object Detection in Adverse Weather Conditions: ECL-YOLOv11 for Automotive Vision Systems. Authors: Zhaohui Liu, Jiaxu Zhang, Xiaojun Zhang and Hongle Song. Affiliation: College of Transportation, Shandong University of Science and Technology, Qingdao 266590, China. Correspondence: zhaohuiliu@sdust.edu.cn. Abstract: The rapid development of intelligent transportation systems and autonomous driving technologies has made visual perception a key component in ensuring safety and improving efficiency in complex traffic environments. As a core task in visual perception, object detection directly affects the reliability of downstream modules such as path planning and decision control. However, adverse weather conditions significantly degrade image quality, causing texture blurring, reduced contrast, and increased noise, which weakens the robustness of traditional detection models and raises potential traffic safety risks. To address this challenge, this paper proposes an enhanced object detection framework, ECL-YOLOv11, designed to improve detection accuracy and real-time performance under adverse weather conditions. The architecture integrates three key modules: a Convolutional Edge-enhancement module that fuses edge features extracted by Sobel operators with convolutional features to explicitly retain boundary and contour information; a Context-guided Multi-scale Fusion Network that enhances perception of small and distant objects through multi-scale feature integration and context modeling; and a Lightweight Shared Convolutional Detection Head that adopts shared convolutions and GroupNorm normalization to optimize computational efficiency. Experimental results show that ECL-YOLOv11 achieves mAP@50 and mAP@50–95 values of 62.7% and 40.5%, respectively, representing improvements over the baseline YOLOv11, while the Precision reaches 73.1%. The model achieves a balanced trade-off between accuracy and inference speed, operating at 237.8 FPS on standard hardware.

sections.title: Background Motivation
sections.content: With the rapid development of intelligent transportation systems and autonomous driving technologies, visual perception has become one of the core technologies for ensuring safety and improving efficiency in complex traffic environments. Object detection, as a key task in visual perception, directly impacts the reliability of downstream functions such as path planning and decision control. However, in practical applications, adverse weather conditions such as fog, rain, and snow remain a significant challenge for object detection. These weather factors significantly degrade image quality, causing blurriness, reduced contrast, and increased noise, which severely weakens the robustness of traditional object detection frameworks. In low-visibility environments, stable detection of vehicles and pedestrians is particularly crucial, as detection failures can directly lead to traffic safety incidents. In recent years, object detection methods based on convolutional neural networks have achieved remarkable progress in conventional scenarios, attaining a relatively balanced trade-off between detection accuracy and real-time performance. However, when visibility decreases significantly, these models often find it difficult to effectively preserve edge and texture features, resulting in blurred object boundaries, missed small targets, and category confusion. In addition, the stringent real-time requirements of automotive platforms mean that complex or high-parameter detection models can easily cause inference latency issues. Transformer-based detection models can model global dependencies within large receptive fields, thereby achieving stronger semantic consistency in complex backgrounds. Despite their superior performance in multi-class detection scenarios, Transformer-based models are characterized by enormous computational demands and high training costs, which pose significant challenges for real-time inference in vehicle-mounted systems. Research on object detection under adverse weather generally falls into two major categories: image enhancement or dehazing-based preprocessing approaches, and architectural improvements to detection models. The former can improve image visibility but inevitably increase computational overhead. The latter enhances robustness through domain adaptation, feature decoupling, or multi-scale fusion mechanisms, but typically require more complex feature pyramids or multi-branch inference structures, which compromise real-time performance. Therefore, improving the robustness of detection models under adverse weather conditions while maintaining high inference efficiency has become a key challenge for intelligent driving vision systems.

sections.title: Proposed Method
sections.content: This study proposes an enhanced object detection framework, ECL-YOLOv11, aiming to solve the robustness and real-time challenges of object detection under adverse weather conditions. Compared to the traditional YOLOv11, ECL-YOLOv11 introduces three structural improvements. First, the Edge-Enhancement Convolution module is integrated into the Backbone to preserve edge and contour information in images. In adverse weather conditions, image contrast and clarity often significantly decrease. The degradation of edge and texture information makes it difficult to accurately identify object boundaries. The CE module introduces a fixed Sobel operator to extract horizontal and vertical gradients, which are then fused with learnable convolutional features. This explicitly retains edge information in the network's feature layer, achieving dual representation of texture and semantic features. The module comprises two parallel branches: the Sobel edge extraction branch and the learnable convolutional branch. These features are concatenated across channels and then compressed and fused via convolutions. Second, in the Neck, the Context-Guided Multi-Scale Fusion Network is designed to enhance the model's capability of perceiving multi-scale features through context guidance. AENet replaces the Neck component of the original YOLOv11. Its architecture comprises four functional sub-modules: Pyramid Context Extraction, Rectangular Calibration, Down-to-Up Information Flow, and Feedback Block. These modules work through hierarchical complementarity and contextual coupling mechanisms, enabling the model to simultaneously enhance global semantic understanding and local structural details. The Rectangular Calibration Module adopts a strip-convolution architecture to model long-range dependencies along both the horizontal and vertical directions, thereby capturing the elongated edge structures of rectangular targets. Third, the Lightweight Shared Convolution Detection Head in the Head reduces redundant computations and improves real-time inference efficiency. The core concept of LDHead simplifies the architecture through cross-scale parameter sharing: sharing a unified set of convolutional weights across multi-scale feature maps, thereby maintaining representational power while substantially reducing computational complexity. Additionally, LDHead employs depthwise separable convolution and GroupNorm normalization strategies to achieve efficient feature modeling and stable distribution alignment. These three modules are structurally complementary, corresponding respectively to edge preservation, context fusion, and computational optimization, forming an integrated architecture for object detection under adverse weather conditions.

sections.title: Experimental Results
sections.content: This study utilizes a self-developed dataset of severe weather traffic scenarios, comprising 9006 road traffic images captured under three typical meteorological conditions: rain, fog, and snow. The images were acquired using vehicle-mounted high-definition cameras, covering urban roads and highways with varying lighting conditions, visibility levels, and complex backgrounds. The dataset encompasses seven categories of traffic participants, including bicycles, buses, cars, pedestrians, trains, and trucks. The experimental setup includes an Intel Core i5-12400F CPU and NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 GPU. To comprehensively validate the effectiveness of the ECL-YOLOv11 model, we evaluate three key metrics: mAP, Precision, and Recall. ECL-YOLOv11 attains 62.7% mAP@50 and 40.5% mAP@50–95. Compared with YOLOv11, the gains indicate improved robustness and generalization, with more stable behavior in complex weather. In terms of Precision, ECL-YOLOv11 reaches 73.1%, demonstrating effective reduction of false positives and class confusion under edge blurring, uneven illumination, and rain/fog occlusion. Ablation experiments were conducted to visually demonstrate the effectiveness of the improved modules. An overall mAP improvement of 1.3% was consistently observed across multiple independent experiments. When the CE module was introduced, mAP@50 increased, indicating that edge-enhanced convolution effectively preserves texture details and improves boundary localization accuracy. Introducing AENet further strengthens feature fusion, demonstrating that multi-scale semantic integration effectively improves overall detection accuracy. The LDHead module introduces a decoupling mechanism in the detection head, enabling more independent classification and regression. Comparison experiments show that ECL-YOLOv11 exhibits significant superiority in the object detection task compared to YOLOv11, YOLOv10n, YOLOv8, RT-DETR, and Faster R-CNN. ECL-YOLOv11 achieves 62.7% mAP@50 and 40.5% mAP@50–95 with 73.1% Precision and 55.6% Recall, outperforming the compared YOLO-series baselines. Compared with non-YOLO detectors such as RT-DETR and Faster R-CNN, ECL-YOLOv11 attains comparable accuracy while delivering significantly faster inference. Qualitative visualizations demonstrate that ECL-YOLOv11 maintains high-confidence detections across varying motion states and adverse weather conditions, avoiding category confusion and missed detections.

sections.title: Conclusion Future
sections.content: This study presents ECL-YOLOv11, an edge-enhanced, context-guided, and lightweight object detection framework designed for vehicle-mounted visual perception under adverse weather conditions. Building upon the YOLOv11 baseline, the proposed model integrates three complementary modules: the Edge-Enhancement Convolution module, which explicitly preserves edge and gradient features to mitigate boundary degradation under low visibility; the Context-Guided Multi-Scale Fusion Network, which strengthens semantic consistency and multi-scale representation through context-aware feature aggregation; and the Lightweight Shared-Convolution Detection Head, which optimizes computational paths for real-time inference without sacrificing accuracy. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that ECL-YOLOv11 achieves modest yet stable and reproducible performance improvements in detection accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency compared with mainstream detectors. Specifically, the model reaches mAP@50 = 62.7%, mAP@50–95 = 40.5%, and 237.8 FPS. Under fog, rain, and snow, the framework maintains consistent detection confidence and avoids misclassification or missed targets common to traditional detectors, validating its robust adaptability across complex environmental and motion states. The design philosophy of ECL-YOLOv11 emphasizes a balance between structural interpretability and operational practicality. Nevertheless, several limitations remain. The dataset used in this study is relatively small and focuses on adverse-weather scenarios; systematic evaluations under clear weather and larger-scale data remain to be performed. Additionally, the training process was constrained by computational resources, which may limit the achievable upper bound of model performance. The model also relies solely on visual input, without leveraging complementary modalities. Future research will therefore focus on three directions: Multi-sensor fusion, integrating ECL-YOLOv11 with LiDAR and millimeter-wave radar to improve depth perception and robustness in low-visibility environments; System-level co-optimization, coupling detection, planning, and decision-making modules in autonomous-driving pipelines to enable end-to-end collaborative learning; and Dynamic-scene adaptation, developing online and continual-learning mechanisms to sustain long-term stability under evolving real-world conditions. In summary, ECL-YOLOv11 demonstrates scientifically sound, repeatable, and practically deployable improvements in object detection under complex weather.
